summary: Studies self-improving agents that rewrite both a programmatic policy (policy.py) and their own tests (tests.py) across 10 rounds on Atari games. Self-test scores stay high (>=0.70) while hidden deployment returns stay low or regress. The paper proposes SEAL, a harness-side sealed audit that compares each candidate against the incumbent, returns only accept/reject, and rolls back on regression. SEAL beats unprotected and self-constrained baselines on most model-game cells.

claims.claim: Self-authored verification does not track deployment performance: all valid cells end with self-score >= 0.70, yet many policies are at or below random.
claims.evidence: Table 4: 35 model-game cells with valid self-tests all have self-score >= 0.70; 15/35 score below the game's random reference, including six at Pong's -21.0 floor (Finding 1).

claims.claim: Internal self-test constraints (monotone, discriminative) do not close the gap.
claims.evidence: Table 5 (Breakout, 3 seeds, mean ± half-range): monotone and discriminative fall below 'none' for 4 of 6 models. Half-ranges are large (e.g. Doubao none 19.1 ± 17.9), so many differences fall inside the spread.

claims.claim: SEAL outperforms unprotected baselines across six models and three seeds.
claims.evidence: Table 5: SEAL > none for all 6 Breakout models (e.g. Gemini-3-Flash 7.9 -> 30.0). Doubao SEAL 35.1 ± 26.0 overlaps none (19.1 ± 17.9). Table 7: equal or better in 11/12 cross-game cells, where the Pong 'ties' are both at the -21 floor and one SpaceInvaders cell is lower (310 vs 297).

claims.claim: The gain comes from preventing overwrite, not from extra search.
claims.evidence: Table 6 compute-matched Breakout pilot: 4 models; mean final truth 7.7 (none) vs 15.4 (SEAL); peak-to-final loss 6.9 -> 0.4. Labeled a 'pilot'; seed count not stated in the table.

claims.claim: Hiding audit scores matters: leaking numeric audit scores weakens the gate.
claims.evidence: Table 5 last two columns: SEAL >= leaky-anchor in 6/6 rows, strictly higher in 5. The largest gap (Doubao 35.1 vs 12.7) has a very wide half-range.

patterns.note: Unprotected self-improving loops with self-authored acceptance regress or fail to discover. Self-improvement needs an exogenous acceptance signal.
A fixed, harness-owned execution-based audit (hidden rollouts) used as an accept/reject gate prevents regressions.
Agent-written tests saturate without measuring the deployment distribution, so test-first only works if some of the tests are outside the agent's control.
Sealed, single-bit, conservative acceptance boundary enforced by the harness rather than by the agent.

methodology.sample: 5 Atari games (Breakout, Pong, SpaceInvaders, Seaquest, MsPacman); 10 rounds per run; deployment truth = 5 hidden seeds x 6 episodes. Full condition ablation only on Breakout; cross-game SEAL comparison uses 3 games x 4 models.
methodology.baselines: none, monotone, discriminative, endo-gate, leaky-anchor (all authors' own ablation conditions); no external self-improvement system as a baseline.
methodology.models: 7 named: DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Gemini-3-Flash, MiniMax-M2.7, Doubao-Seed-2.0-Pro, Kimi-K2.5, Qwen3.6-Plus, GPT-5.5 (6 in the Breakout ablation).
methodology.variance: Three seeds, mean ± half-range. Half-ranges are often comparable to effects; no significance tests.
methodology.ablations: Yes: condition matrix, audit leakage, compute-matched pilot.
methodology.contamination_controls: Deployment truth is hidden from the agent and separate from the audit; n/a for training contamination.
methodology.languages: Python policies on Atari; no software-engineering tasks.

standards.artifacts: No code or data link found; proofs and further analysis are deferred to supplementary material that is not in the text.

biases.detail: Atari programmatic policies with sticky-action shift. The transfer to code-editing agents (SWE-style tasks) is argued, not tested.
Three seeds with wide half-ranges; Table 6 is a 4-model 'pilot'; the cross-game comparison is 12 cells.
Only half-ranges; no CIs or tests. Several 'wins' overlap.
No code release is mentioned, and the supplement is referenced but not available in the text.
The cost of audit rollouts and model calls is not reported beyond proposal-count matching.

verdict_reason: The core finding (agent-authored tests saturate while hidden performance stays low) and the SEAL gate are a useful, multi-model, ablated result. However, the domain is Atari, the seeds are few with overlapping spreads, there is no limitations section, and no code is released.
applicability: Directly supports a harness rule the team should adopt with spec-driven development: when an agent writes both the code and its tests, the acceptance gate must include checks the agent cannot author or see. For the Java team, that means spec-derived contract/acceptance tests owned by humans or the spec (e.g. schema and delivery-API contract tests across the several repositories), plus CI gates run by the deterministic CLI, with agents getting pass/fail rather than tuning to the hidden suite. It matches the 'LLM proposes, qr verifies' invariant. Caveat: the evidence comes from Atari policies, not Java services, so treat it as a design principle, not a measured effect size.
